summary: This experimental memo outlines a protocol for connecting hosts running the TCP/IP suite over a SCSI bus, so the cable normally used for disks can carry network traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: Using a cable meant for hard drives as a network cable too.

subtitle: Carrying IP datagrams over SCSI cables to create high-speed local networks.

tldr.problem: High-speed data transfers within clusters of workstations face a gap between local memory/disk speeds (gigabit speeds) and typical local area network speeds (100 Mbps in 1997).
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2143 defines how to encapsulate IP datagrams into SCSI messages using the SCSI 10-byte command header, reusing existing SCSI cables and host adapters for network communication.
tldr.outcome: This allows clusters of closely-spaced machines to communicate at SCSI speeds (around 360 Mbps) using existing hardware, useful for parallel computing and high-speed file services.

today: RFC 2143 is Experimental and purely historical. SCSI as a network medium was never adopted. The idea was superseded by faster local area networks, Gigabit Ethernet, and other technologies that do not require special hardware.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2143 proposes an unusual solution to a real problem: how to create very high-speed networks within small clusters of workstations. The idea is to use the Small Computer System Interface (SCSI), the standard bus normally used to connect hard drives and other peripherals to computers, as a network medium for IP traffic.

SCSI buses can transfer data at speeds approaching 360 megabits per second—much faster than the 100 Mbps local area networks available in 1997—but are limited to short distances (less than 10 meters) and a small number of devices (typically 8 or 16).
sections.plainLanguage: Hard drives connect to computers with cables that can handle lots of data very quickly. This memo says we can use those same cables to make a super-fast network for a small group of computers.

sections.title: Encapsulation in SCSI Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines how to wrap an IP datagram inside a SCSI command message. It uses the SCSI 10-byte SEND_MESSAGE command, which contains a 10-byte header followed by a payload. The header specifies the operation code (0x2A), the logical unit number, the protocol type (using the same values as Ethernet), and the datagram length as a 16-bit number in big-endian format.

This design choice is elegant because the IP datagram length field matches the SCSI transfer length field, and the protocol type field reuses standard Ethernet protocol numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: We take an IP message, put it inside a special SCSI wrapper that labels what kind of data it is and how big it is, then send it down the SCSI cable.

sections.title: Addressing and Scaling
sections.content:
SCSI buses do not support broadcasting, so an Address Resolution Protocol implementation must send queries to each device on the bus in sequence to discover which device has a particular IP address. This is less efficient than Ethernet broadcasting but workable with good ARP caching.

A single SCSI bus supports only a handful of devices, but RFC 2143 shows how to scale by using multiple SCSI host adapters in each machine, creating a mesh or tree topology connected by IP routing. For example, eight machines connected to a single SCSI bus can be linked via another SCSI bus, eventually creating a network of 64 or more machines.
sections.plainLanguage: SCSI buses are small, so you connect multiple SCSI buses together using routers. Each group of computers talks on its own SCSI bus, and the routers pass messages between the buses.

references.text: ANSI X3T9 Technical Committee, "Small Computer System Interface - 2", X3T9.2, Project 375D, Revision 10L, September 1993.
